rulings.headline: Video Review: NSH @ MTL – 19:28 of the Second Period
rulings.result_text: Goal Nashville
rulings.explanation: Video Review confirmed the official’s call on the ice that the actions of Canadiens forward Josh Anderson caused the net to be displaced from its moorings prior to the puck crossing the goal line. Therefore, the Referees awarded a goal to Matthew Wood according to Rule 63.7: “In the event that the goal post is displaced, either deliberately or accidentally, by a defending player, prior to the puck crossing the goal line between the normal position of the goalposts, the Referee may award a goal. In order to award a goal in this situation, the goal post must have been displaced by the actions of a defending player, the attacking player must have an imminent scoring opportunity prior to the goal post being displaced, and it must be determined that the puck would have entered the net between the normal position of the goal posts.”
rulings.basis: statement gives the result but not the on-ice call

rulings.headline: Coach’s Challenge: NSH @ MTL – 1:36 of the First Period
rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is overturned – No Goal Montreal
rulings.explanation:
The play on the ice was challenged under Rule 38 – Coach’s Challenge. Rule 38.1 states, “In all Coach’s Challenge situations, the original call on the ice will be overturned if, and only if, a conclusive and irrefutable determination can be made on the basis of video evidence that the original call on the ice was clearly not correct. If a review is not conclusive and/or there is any doubt whatsoever as to whether the call on the ice was correct, the original call on the ice will be confirmed.”

Video review determined that Montreal’s Chris Kreider preceded the puck into the offensive zone and was in an off-side position prior to his goal. According to Rule 38.9, “The standard for overturning the call in the event of a “GOAL” call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the On-Ice Official(s), determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an “Off-Side” infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed.”

The clock is reset to show 18:41 (1:19 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.
rulings.basis: result line: Call on the ice is overturned – No Goal Montreal

notes: no goal in the final record at the clock; review stoppage present

rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is overturned – No Goal Carolina

Rule 38.1 states, “In all Coach’s Challenge situations, the original call on the ice will be overturned if, and only if, a conclusive and irrefutable determination can be made on the basis of video evidence that the original call on the ice was clearly not correct. If a review is not conclusive and/or there is any doubt whatsoever as to whether the call on the ice was correct, the original call on the ice will be confirmed.”

Video review determined Jordan Staal did not have possession and control of the puck as he entered the attacking zone prior to his goal. The decision was made in accordance with Rule 83.1, which states in part, “a player actually controlling the puck who shall cross the line ahead of the puck shall not be considered ‘off-side,’ provided he had possession and control of the puck prior to his skates crossing the leading edge of the blue line.”  


Additionally, Warren Foegele was assessed a penalty for hooking on a breakaway, therefore, Jordan Martinook was awarded a penalty shot at 3:11 (16:49 elapsed) in accordance with Rule 38.7, which states in part, “If one or more penalties (minor or major) are assessed between the time of the missed infraction and the video review that disallows the apparent goal, the offending team(s) (and responsible Player(s)) will still be required to serve the penalty(ies) identified and assessed, and the time of the penalty(ies) will be recorded as the time at which the play should have been stopped for the missed infraction.”

NOTE: In the final minute of play in the third period and at any point in overtime (regular season and playoffs), Hockey Operations will initiate the review of any scenario that would otherwise be subject to a Coach's Challenge.

The game clock (and penalty clocks, if applicable) will then be re-set to the time of the goal.”

Therefore, the clock is reset to show 10:23 (9:37 elapsed time) and good goal Florida.

rulings.headline: Coach’s Challenge: SJS @ EDM – 0:12 of the Second Period
rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is overturned
rulings.explanation:
The play on the ice was challenged under Rule 38 – Coach’s Challenge. Rule 38.1 states, “In all Coach’s Challenge situations, the original call on the ice will be overturned if, and only if, a conclusive and irrefutable determination can be made on the basis of video evidence that the original call on the ice was clearly not correct. If a review is not conclusive and/or there is any doubt whatsoever as to whether the call on the ice was correct, the original call on the ice will be confirmed."

After a thorough examination of all available replays, video review determined that Darnell Nurse’s shot from the defending zone subsequently deflected off the glass before going out of play in the neutral zone at 19:48 (0:12 elapsed time) of the second period. The decision was made in accordance with Rule 38.2 (d) which states, in part, that a team may request a Coach’s Challenge “When a minor penalty for delaying the game has been assessed under Rule 63.2 (iii) for shooting or batting the puck out of play from the defending zone. This will only apply to delay of game penalties when the shot/batted puck is determined to have subsequently deflected off a player, stick, glass or boards, etc., and not a judgment call.”

Therefore, the delay of game penalty assessed to Darnell Nurse was rescinded.
rulings.basis: result line: Call on the ice is overturned

notes: final call unknown; nothing to compare

rulings.explanation:
Video review determined that the puck shot by Johnathan Kovacevic deflected off of Emil Heineman’s stick before going out of play in the defending zone at 18:39 (1:21 elapsed time). The decision was made in accordance with Rule 38.2 (d) which states, in part, that a team may request a Coach’s Challenge “When a minor penalty for delaying the game has been assessed under Rule 63.2 (iii) for shooting or batting the puck out of play from the defending zone. This will only apply to delay of game penalties when the shot/batted puck is determined to have subsequently deflected off a player, stick, glass or boards, etc., and not a judgment call.”

Therefore, the delay of game penalty assessed to New Jersey was rescinded.

rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is overturned \- No Goal Los Angeles
rulings.explanation: Video review determined Los Angeles’ Joel Edmundson used his glove to bat the puck, which caused the puck to illegally enter the San Jose net. According to Rule 78.5 (i), apparent goals shall be disallowed, “When the puck has been directed, batted or thrown into the net by an attacking player other than with a stick. When this occurs, if it is deemed to be done deliberately, then the decision shall be NO GOAL. A goal cannot be scored when the puck has been deliberately batted with any part of the attacking player’s body into the net.”

rulings.headline: Coach’s Challenge: OTT @ UTA – 5:42 of the Third Period
rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is confirmed – goal Utah
rulings.explanation:
The play on the ice was challenged under Rule 38 – Coach’s Challenge. Rule 38.1 states, “In all Coach’s Challenge situations, the original call on the ice will be overturned if, and only if, a conclusive and irrefutable determination can be made on the basis of video evidence that the original call on the ice was clearly not correct. If a review is not conclusive and/or there is any doubt whatsoever as to whether the call on the ice was correct, the original call on the ice will be confirmed.”

Video review confirmed no goaltender interference infractions occurred as Daniil But was making a play on the loose puck in the crease. The decision was made in accordance with Rule 69.7 which states, in part, the goal on the ice should have been allowed because "in a rebound situation, or where a goalkeeper and attacking player(s) are simultaneously attempting to play a loose puck, whether inside or outside the crease, incidental contact will be permitted, and any goal that is scored as a result thereof will be allowed."

Penalty: 2:00 minor penalty: Delay of Game – Unsuccessful Challenge
rulings.basis: result line: Call on the ice is confirmed – goal Utah

rulings.explanation: In the final minute of play in the third period and at any point in overtime (regular season and playoffs), the NHL Situation Room will initiate the review of any scenario that would otherwise be subject to a Coach’s Challenge under Rule 38.3.There was no conclusive video evidence showing that the puck made contact with Matt Boldy’s stick, therefore, the Situation Room supported the Referees’ call on the ice. rulings.headline: Coach’s Challenge: SJS @ DAL – 17:40 of the Third Period
rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is overturned – No Goal San Jose
rulings.explanation:
The play on the ice was challenged under Rule 38 – Coach’s Challenge. Rule 38.1 states, “In all Coach’s Challenge situations, the original call on the ice will be overturned if, and only if, a conclusive and irrefutable determination can be made on the basis of video evidence that the original call on the ice was clearly not correct. If a review is not conclusive and/or there is any doubt whatsoever as to whether the call on the ice was correct, the original call on the ice will be confirmed.”  
  
Video review determined that San Jose’s Philipp Kurashev preceded the puck into the offensive zone and was in an off-side position prior to Macklin Celebrini’s goal. According to Rule 38.9, “The standard for overturning the call in the event of a “GOAL” call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the On-Ice Official(s), determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an “Off-Side” infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed.”  
  
The clock is reset to show 2:44 (17:16 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.
rulings.basis: result line: Call on the ice is overturned – No Goal San Jose

rulings.headline: Coach’s Challenge: VAN @ TBL – 12:16 of the Third Period
rulings.review_type: Missed Game Stoppage Event – High-Sticking the Puck
rulings.result_text: Original call overturned – No Goal Tampa Bay
rulings.explanation:
The Situation Room determined that Jake Guentzel’s stick contacted the puck above the normal height of his shoulders with 8:14 on the clock (11:46 elapsed time), 30 seconds prior to [Charle-Edouard D'Astous](https://www.nhl.com/lightning/player/charle-edouard-d-astous-8480426)’ goal. The decision was made in accordance with Rule 80.1, which states, in part, that “Batting the puck above the normal height of the shoulders with a stick is prohibited. When a puck is struck with a high stick and subsequently comes into the possession and control of a player from the offending team (including the player who made contact with the puck), either directly or deflected off any player or official, there shall be a whistle.”

Therefore, the clock is reset to show 8:14 (11:46 elapsed time) and no goal Tampa Bay.

rulings.headline: Video Review: NSH @ MIN – 3:38 of Overtime
rulings.result_text: Goal Minnesota
rulings.explanation:
Video review supported the Referees’ call on the ice that the actions of Nashville’s Justus Annunen caused the net to be displaced prior to the puck crossing the goal line. Therefore, the Referees awarded Minnesota’s Marcus Johansson with a goal.

The decision was made in accordance with Rule 63.7 which states “In the event that the goal post is displaced, either deliberately or accidentally, by a defending player, prior to the puck crossing the goal line between the normal position of the goalposts, the Referee may award a goal. In order to award a goal in this situation, the goal post must have been displaced by the actions of a defending player, the attacking player must have an imminent scoring opportunity prior to the goal post being displaced, and it must be determined that the puck would have entered the net between the normal position of the goal posts.”

\-\-\-
rulings.basis: verdict sentence: call stands / confirmed

A goal cannot be scored when the puck has been deliberately batted with any part of the attacking player’s body into the net.”

rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is overturned – No Goal Colorado
rulings.explanation:
Video review determined that Colorado’s Martin Necas preceded the puck into the offensive zone and was in an off-side position prior to his goal. According to Rule 38.9, “The standard for overturning the call in the event of a “GOAL” call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the On-Ice Official(s), determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an “Off-Side” infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed.”

The clock is reset to show 12:47 (7:13 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.
rulings.basis: result line: Call on the ice is overturned – No Goal Colorado

rulings.headline: Coach’s Challenge: EDM @ LAK – 8:53 of the Third Period
rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is upheld
rulings.explanation:
After a thorough examination of all available replays, there was no conclusive evidence that the puck shot by Jake Walman at 11:07 (8:53 elapsed time) deflected off the glass before going out of play. Therefore, the call on the ice stands. The decision was made in accordance with Rule 38.2 (d) which states, in part, that a team may request a Coach’s Challenge “When a minor penalty for delaying the game has been assessed under Rule 63.2 (iii) for shooting or batting the puck out of play from the defending zone. This will only apply to delay of game penalties when the shot/batted puck is determined to have subsequently deflected off a player, stick, glass or boards, etc., and not a judgment call.”

Therefore, an additional minor penalty was assessed to Edmonton (in addition to the existing delay of game penalty).
rulings.basis: result line: Call on the ice is upheld

rulings.headline: Coach’s Challenge: WSH @ PIT – 10:28 of the Second Period
rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is overturned – No Goal Washington
rulings.explanation:
Video review determined that Washington’s Alex Ovechkin preceded the puck into the offensive zone and was in an off-side position prior to Dylan Strome’s goal. According to Rule 38.9, “The standard for overturning the call in the event of a “GOAL” call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the On-Ice Official(s), determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an “Off-Side” infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed.”  
  
The clock is reset to show 9:35 (10:35 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.
rulings.basis: result line: Call on the ice is overturned – No Goal Washington

According to Rule 69.3, “If an attacking player initiates contact with a goalkeeper, incidental or otherwise, while the goalkeeper is in his goal crease, and a goal is scored, the goal will be disallowed.” The decision was also made in accordance with Rule 69.1, which states in part, “The overriding rationale of this rule is that a goalkeeper should have the ability to move freely within his goal crease without being hindered by the actions of an attacking player. rulings.explanation:

The decision was made in accordance with Rule 38.2 (d) which states, in part, that a team may request a Coach’s Challenge “When a minor penalty for delaying the game has been assessed under Rule 63.2 (iii) for shooting or batting the puck out of play from the defending zone. This will only apply to delay of game penalties when the shot/batted puck is determined to have subsequently deflected off a player, stick, glass or boards, etc., and not a judgment call.”  
  
Therefore, the delay of game penalty assessed to Washington was rescinded.

rulings.headline: Situation Room Initiated Challenge: OTT @ CHI – 0:46 of Overtime
rulings.result_text: Goal Ottawa
rulings.explanation:
Video review supported the Referee’s call on the ice that the puck deflected off of Tim Stützle’s skate and entered the net in a legal fashion. Further, a challenge initiated by the Situation Room for goaltender interference determined that the actions of Chicago’s Wyatt Kaiser caused Stützle to contact goaltender Arvid Soderblom prior to his goal. Rule 37.4 states, in part, “a puck that deflects into the net off an attacking Player’s skate who does not use a ‘distinct kicking motion’ shall be ruled a GOAL. A puck that is directed into the net by an attacking Players’ skate shall also be ruled a GOAL, as long as no ‘distinct kicking motion’ is evident.” Rule 69.1 states, “If an attacking player has been pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending player so as to cause him to come into contact with the goalkeeper, such contact will not be deemed contact initiated by the attacking player for purposes of this rule, provided the attacking player has made a reasonable effort to avoid such contact.”  
  
NOTE: In the final minute of play in the third period and at any point in overtime (regular season and playoffs), Hockey Operations will initiate the review of any scenario that would otherwise be subject to a Coach's Challenge.

\-\-\-

rulings.headline: Coach’s Challenge: COL @ CGY – 19:32 of the First Period
rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is overturned – No Goal Colorado
rulings.explanation:
Video review determined that Colorado’s Jonathan Drouin preceded the puck into the offensive zone and was in an off-side position prior to Sam Malinski’s goal. According to Rule 38.9, “The standard for overturning the call in the event of a “GOAL” call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the On-Ice Official(s), determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an “Off-Side” infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed.”

The clock is reset to show 0:34 (19:26 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.
rulings.basis: result line: Call on the ice is overturned – No Goal Colorado

rulings.result_text: Call on the ice confirmed – No goal New Jersey

The on-ice officials first huddled and determined the call on the ice would be “no goal”. Video review then confirmed that Ondrej Palat’s stick was above the height of the crossbar when he deflected the puck into the Vegas net. According to Rule 78.5 (vi) that states in part “Apparent goals shall be disallowed by the Referee . . . Where the puck makes contact with the stick is the determining factor.”

According to Rule 69.3, “If an attacking player initiates contact with a goalkeeper, incidental or otherwise, while the goalkeeper is in his goal crease, and a goal is scored, the goal will be disallowed.”

rulings.headline: Coach’s Challenge: CBJ @ UTA – 6:58 of the First Period
rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is overturned
rulings.explanation:
After a thorough examination of all available replays, video review determined that the batted puck by Daniil Tarasov subsequently deflected off Lawson Crouse’s glove before going out of play in the defending zone at 13:02 (6:58 elapsed time). The decision was made in accordance with Rule 38.2 (d) which states, in part, that a team may request a Coach’s Challenge “When a minor penalty for delaying the game has been assessed under Rule 63.2 (iii) for shooting or batting the puck out of play from the defending zone. This will only apply to delay of game penalties when the shot/batted puck is determined to have subsequently deflected off a player, stick, glass or boards, etc., and not a judgment call.”

Therefore, the delay of game penalty assessed to Columbus was rescinded.
rulings.basis: result line: Call on the ice is overturned

notes: final call unknown; nothing to compare

rulings.headline: Coach’s Challenge: CAR @ DAL – 13:08 of the Third Period
rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is overturned
rulings.explanation:
After a thorough examination of all available replays, video review determined that Brendan Smith’s pass subsequently deflected off Jesperi Kotkaniemi’s stick before going out of play in the defending zone at 6:12 (13:48 elapsed time). The decision was made in accordance with Rule 38.2 (d) which states, in part, that a team may request a Coach’s Challenge “When a minor penalty for delaying the game has been assessed under Rule 63.2 (iii) for shooting or batting the puck out of play from the defending zone. This will only apply to delay of game penalties when the shot/batted puck is determined to have subsequently deflected off a player, stick, glass or boards, etc., and not a judgment call.”  
  
Therefore, the delay of game penalty assessed to Brendan Smith was rescinded.
rulings.basis: result line: Call on the ice is overturned

rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is overturned – No Goal Carolina
rulings.explanation:
Video review determined that Carolina’s Jackson Blake preceded the puck into the offensive zone and was in the process of exiting the ice, however, his skate was still touching the ice when Sebastian Aho entered the offensive zone, therefore, the delayed off-side remained in effect. According to Rule 38.9, “The standard for overturning the call in the event of a “GOAL” call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the On-Ice Official(s), determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an “Off-Side” infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed.”  
  
Additionally, according to Rule 83.3, “If, during a delayed off-side, an attacking player in the attacking zone elects to proceed to his players’ bench (which extends into the attacking zone) to be replaced by a teammate, he shall be considered to have cleared the zone when both skates are off the ice and the Linesman judges him to have left the playing surface.”  
  
The clock is reset to show 5:11 (14:49 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.
rulings.basis: result line: Call on the ice is overturned – No Goal Carolina

According to Rule 78.5 (i), apparent goals shall be disallowed, “When the puck has been directed, batted or thrown into the net by an attacking player other than with a stick. This will only apply to delay of game penalties when the shot/batted puck is determined to have subsequently deflected off a player, stick, glass or boards, etc., and not a judgment call.”

Therefore, the delay of game penalty assessed to Jack Quinn was rescinded.

According to Rule 38.9, “The standard for overturning the call in the event of a “GOAL” call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the On-Ice Official(s), determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an “Off-Side” infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed.”

According to Rule 38.9, “The standard for overturning the call in the event of a “GOAL” call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the On-Ice Official(s), determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an “Off-Side” infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed.”

The clock is reset to show 10:53 (9:07 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.

Therefore, the clock is reset to show 18:32 (1:28 elapsed time) and good goal Dallas.

Video review determined that Tampa Bay’s Anthony Cirelli preceded the puck into the offensive zone without possession and control and, therefore, was in an off-side position prior to Brandon Hagel’s goal. According to Rule 38.9, “The standard for overturning the call in the event of a “GOAL” call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the On-Ice Official(s), determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an “Off-Side” infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed.”

The clock is reset to show 19:25 (0:35 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.

rulings.headline: Video Review: FLA @ TOR -- Shootout
rulings.result_text: No Goal Florida
rulings.explanation:
The Situation Room initiated a video review to further examine whether Evan Rodrigues’ shootout attempt entered the Toronto net in a legal fashion. Video review determined Rodrigues’ shot crossed the Toronto goal line as a result of a rebound. According to Rule 37.3 (j), “The legitimacy of all potential goals on Penalty Shot or Shootout attempts to ensure compliance with applicable rules (e.g., double tap, goalkeeper throwing stick, goalkeeper dislodging goal, shooter cradling puck above the normal height of the shoulders, shooter performing illegal spin-o-rama move, skater’s continued forward advancement of puck, goalkeeper leaving crease prior to puck touch at center ice, etc.).

This is also covered by Rule 24.2, which states in part: “No goal can be scored on a rebound of any kind (an exception being the puck off the goal post or crossbar, then the goalkeeper and then directly into the goal), and any time the puck crosses the goal line or comes to a complete stop, the shot shall be considered complete.”
rulings.basis: statement gives the result but not the on-ice call

rulings.headline: Video Review/Coach’s Challenge: BUF @ NYI – 13:40 of the Third Period
rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is upheld – Goal NY Islanders
rulings.explanation:
Video review confirmed that  Casey Cizikas’ stick was at or below the height of the crossbar when he directed the puck into the Buffalo net. According to Rule 37.5, “If the puck makes contact with a portion of the stick that is at or below the level of the crossbar (despite some other portion of the stick being above the crossbar) and enters the goal, the goal shall be allowed.”

Buffalo then initiated a Coach’s Challenge for Off-Side. Video review confirmed that Noah Dobson had possession and control of the puck as he entered the attacking zone prior to Cizikas’ goal. Rule 83.1 states, in part, that “a player actually controlling the puck who shall cross the line ahead of the puck shall not be considered ‘off-side,’ provided he had possession and control of the puck prior to his skates crossing the leading edge of the blue line.”

Penalty: 2:00 minor penalty: Delay of Game – Unsuccessful Challenge
rulings.basis: result line: Call on the ice is upheld – Goal NY Islanders

rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is overturned – No Goal Seattle
rulings.explanation: Video review determined Seattle’s Jared McCann impaired Jordan Binnington’s ability to play his position in the crease prior to Vince Dunn’s goal. The decision was made in accordance with Rule 69.1 which states, in part, “Goals should be disallowed only if: (1) an attacking player, either by his positioning or by contact, impairs the goalkeeper’s ability to move freely within his crease or defend his goal. For purposes of this rule, ‘contact,’ whether incidental or otherwise, shall mean any contact that is made between or among a goalkeeper and attacking player(s), whether by means of a stick or any part of the body.”

rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is overturned – No Goal NY Rangers
rulings.explanation:

According to Rule 38.9, “The standard for overturning the call in the event of a “GOAL” call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the On-Ice Official(s), determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an “Off-Side” infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed.”

The clock is reset to show 9:14 (10:46 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.
rulings.basis: result line: Call on the ice is overturned – No Goal NY Rangers

rulings.headline: Video Review: SEA @ DAL - 11:37 of the Third Period
rulings.result_text: Goal Dallas
rulings.explanation:
The Situation Room informed the off-ice officials to sound the in-arena horn after it was confirmed that Roope Hintz's shot at 11:20 completely crossed the Seattle goal line. According to Rule 37.6, "Should the NHL Situation Room be able to determine that a goal has been scored through the use of video replay, and play on the ice has nonetheless continued, the NHL Situation Room shall instruct that the in-arena horn be sounded to stop play immediately, and the goal will be awarded. rulings.headline: Video Review: CBJ @ MTL - 18:00 of the First Period
rulings.result_text: Goal Columbus
rulings.explanation: Video Review determined that Montreal goaltender Sam Montembeault caused the net to be displaced from its moorings prior to the puck crossing the goal line. Therefore, the Referees awarded Blue Jackets forward Kirill Marchenko a goal. The decision was made in accordance with Rule 63.7, which states, in part, that "In the event that the goal post is displaced, either deliberately or accidentally, by a defending player, prior to the puck crossing the goal line between the normal position of the goalposts, the Referee may award a goal. In order to award a goal in this situation, the goal post must have been displaced by the actions of a defending player, the attacking player must have an imminent scoring opportunity prior to the goal post being displaced, and it must be determined that the puck would have entered the net between the normal position of the goal posts."

rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is overturned - Goal Arizona
rulings.explanation:
The Situation Room initiated a video review to examine if the puck entered the St. Louis net in a legal fashion. Video review determined that Nick Schmaltz had an imminent scoring opportunity prior to the goal posts being displaced by Brayden Schenn and the puck entered the St. Louis net between the normal position of the goal posts.
The decision was made in accordance with Rule 63.7, which states, in part, that "In the event that the goal post is displaced, either deliberately or accidentally, by a defending player, prior to the puck crossing the goal line between the normal position of the goalposts, the Referee may award a goal. In order to award a goal in this situation, the goal post must have been displaced by the actions of a defending player, the attacking player must have an imminent scoring opportunity prior to the goal post being displaced, and it must be determined that the puck would have entered the net between the normal position of the goal posts."

rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is upheld - Goal Toronto
rulings.explanation:
The Situation Room initiated a video review to examine if the puck entered the Florida net in a legal fashion. Video review determined that Auston Matthews had an imminent scoring opportunity prior to the goal posts being displaced and, therefore, the puck entered the Florida net in a legal fashion.
The decision was made in accordance with Rule 63.7, which states, in part, that "In the event that the goal post is displaced, either deliberately or accidentally, by a defending player, prior to the puck crossing the goal line between the normal position of the goalposts, the Referee may award a goal. In order to award a goal in this situation, the goal post must have been displaced by the actions of a defending player, the attacking player must have an imminent scoring opportunity prior to the goal post being displaced, and it must be determined that the puck would have entered the net between the normal position of the goal posts."

rulings.result_text: Original call is upheld - Goal Montreal
rulings.explanation:
Video review confirmed that Christian Dvorak's stick was at or below the height of the crossbar when he directed the puck into the Blues net. According to Rule 37.5,"If the puck makes contact with a portion of the stick that is at or below the level of the crossbar (despite some other portion of the stick being above the crossbar) and enters the goal, the goal shall be allowed."
NOTE:The Referee mistakenly announced St. Louis had initiated a Coach's Challenge to examine the high-sticking play. However, high-sticking the puck into the net is not a challengeable play as per Rule 38.2, which states in part,"A team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios: (a) "Off-Side" Play Leading to a Goal . . . (b) Missed Game Stoppage Event in the Offensive Zone Leading to a Goal . . . (c) Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper."
rulings.basis: result line: Original call is upheld - Goal Montreal

rulings.headline: Situation Room Initiated Challenge: ARI @ TOR - 19:21 of the Third Period
rulings.review_type: Missed Game Stoppage Event - Hand Pass
rulings.result_text: Original call overturned - No Goal Toronto
rulings.explanation:
The Situation Room determined that Morgan Rielly batted the puck with his hand inside the attacking zone before teammate Mitchell Marner subsequently gained possession and control. According to Rule 79.1, a player may bat a puck in the air with his open hand, "unless, in the opinion of the on-ice officials, he has directed the puck to a teammate, or has allowed his team to gain an advantage, and subsequently possession and control of the puck is obtained by a player of the offending team, either directly or deflected off any player or official." In this case, it was deemed that Marner was the first player to gain possession and control of the puck after Rielly batted it with his hand.
NOTE:In the final minute of play in the third period and at any point in overtime (regular season and playoffs), Hockey Operations will initiate the review of any scenario that would otherwise be subject to a Coach's Challenge.
rulings.basis: result line: Original call overturned - No Goal Toronto

According to Rule 38.9, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a "GOAL" call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the On-Ice Official(s), determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an "Off-Side" infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed."
The clock is reset to show 15:28 (4:32 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.

rulings.result_text: Goal Pittsburgh
rulings.explanation: Video Review determined that the actions of Patrik Nemeth caused the net to be displaced from its moorings prior to the puck crossing the goal line. rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is overturned - No Goal Carolina
rulings.explanation:
Video review determined that Carolina's Andrei Svechnikov preceded the puck into the offensive zone and was in an off-side position prior to Brett Pesce's goal. According to Rule 38.9, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a "GOAL" call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the On-Ice Official(s), determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an "Off-Side" infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed."
The clock is reset to show 17:01 (2:59 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.

rulings.review_type: Puck Over Goal Line and High-Sticking the Puck
rulings.result_text: No Goal Philadelphia
rulings.explanation:
At 17:20 elapsed time, the Situation Room informed the off-ice officials to sound the in-arena horn after it was confirmed that the puck entered the Tampa Bay net at 16:50 (3:10 on the clock). This was done in accordance with Rule 37.6.
Upon further review, it was determined that Scott Laughton's stick was above the height of the crossbar when he directed the puck into the net. According to Rule 80.3, "When an attacking player causes the puck to enter the opponent's goal by contacting the puck above the height of the crossbar, either directly or deflected off any player or official, the goal shall not be allowed. The determining factor is where the puck makes contact with the stick. If the puck makes contact with the stick at or below the level of the crossbar and enters the goal, this goal shall be allowed."
Therefore, no goal Philadelphia and the clock is reset to show 3:10 (16:50 elapsed time) - when the puck originally crossed the goal line.

rulings.result_text: Goal Ottawa
rulings.explanation: Video Review confirmed that the actions of Avalanche defenseman Jack Johnson caused the net to be displaced from its moorings prior to the puck crossing the goal line. Therefore, the Referees awarded Senators forward Tim Stützle a goal according to Rule 63.7: "In the event that the goal post is displaced, either deliberately or accidentally, by a defending player, prior to the puck crossing the goal line between the normal position of the goalposts, the Referee may award a goal. In order to award a goal in this situation, the goal post must have been displaced by the actions of a defending player, the attacking player must have an imminent scoring opportunity prior to the goal post being displaced, and it must be determined that the puck would have entered the net between the normal position of the goal posts."

rulings.headline: Video Review: BOS @ TOR - 12:21 of the First Period
rulings.result_text: Goal Toronto
rulings.explanation:
The Referee's call on the ice was that the puck crossed the Boston goal line after the actions of Patrice Bergeron caused the net to be displaced. Video review upheld the Referee's call on the ice.
The decision was made in accordance with Rule 63.7 which states, in part, that "in the event that the goal post is displaced, either deliberately or accidentally, by a defending player, prior to the puck crossing the goal line between the normal position of the goalposts, the Referee may award a goal. In order to award a goal in this situation, the goal post must have been displaced by the actions of a defending player, the attacking player must have an imminent scoring opportunity prior to the goal post being displaced, and it must be determined that the puck would have entered the net between the normal position of the goal posts."
rulings.basis: verdict sentence: call stands / confirmed

rulings.headline: Coach's Challenge: TBL @ OTT - 5:16 of the Second Period
rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is confirmed - "No Goal" due to Goaltender Interference
rulings.explanation:
Video review determined that the actions of Lightning forward Steven Stamkos caused Senators defenseman Artem Zub to contact his own goaltender, supporting the "no goal" due to goaltender interference call originally made on the ice.
Per Rule 69.1: If a defending player has been pushed, shoved, or fouled by an attacking player so as to cause the defending player to come into contact with his own goalkeeper, such contact shall be deemed contact initiated by the attacking player for purposes of this rule, and if necessary a penalty assessed to the attacking player and if a goal is scored it would be disallowed.
rulings.basis: result line: Call on the ice is confirmed - "No Goal" due to Goaltender Interference

rulings.explanation: At 18:44 of the first period in the Predators/Hurricanes game, a double-minor penalty was assessed to Carolina's Andrei Svechnikov. After reviewing the play, the referees determined that it was the stick of Nashville's Mattias Ekholm - and not Svechnikov's - that originally struck Eeli Tolvanen. Rule 60.3 states that when a double-minor is called for high-sticking, the referee "shall have the option (but not the obligation) to review video of the play for the purpose of confirming (or not) their original call on the ice, and, in particular, whether the stick causing the apparent injury was actually the stick of the Player being penalized." The video review process cannot be used to assess any other penalties.

rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is upheld - Goal Dallas
rulings.explanation:
Video review confirmed the Referee's call on the ice that the actions of Nashville goaltender Pekka Rinne caused the goalpost to be displaced prior to the puck crossing the goal line between the normal position of the goalposts.
Therefore, the Referees awarded a goal to Dallas' Joe Pavelski. The decision was made in accordance with Rule 63.7 which states, in part, that "in the event that the goal post is displaced, either deliberately or accidentally, by a defending player, prior to the puck crossing the goal line between the normal position of the goalposts, the Referee may award a goal. In order to award a goal in this situation, the goal post must have been displaced by the actions of a defending player, the attacking player must have an imminent scoring opportunity prior to the goal post being displaced, and it must be determined that the puck would have entered the net between the normal position of the goal posts."

rulings.headline: Video Review: ANA @ ARI - 12:02 of the Second Period
rulings.review_type: Distinct Kicking Motion and Net Off Its Moorings
rulings.result_text: Goal Arizona
rulings.explanation:
Video review supported the Referee's call on the ice that the puck deflected off of Jakob Chychrun's skate and entered the net in a legal fashion. Rule 37.4 states, in part, "A puck that deflects into the net off an attacking Player's skate who does not use a "distinct kicking motion" shall be ruled a GOAL. A puck that is directed into the net by an attacking Players' skate shall also be ruled a GOAL, as long as no "distinct kicking motion" is evident."
Additionally, video review supported the Referee's call on the ice that Jakob Chychrun's shot completely crossed the Anaheim goal line prior to the net coming off of its moorings.
rulings.description: Good goal Arizona
rulings.basis: verdict sentence: call stands / confirmed

rulings.headline: Coach's Challenge Clarification: CAR @ CBJ - 18:45 of the Second Period
rulings.explanation:
Columbus requested a coach's challenge for off-side prior to a goal at 18:45 of the second period.

During the review, a miscommunication occurred between the Video Replay Booth in Columbus, the Linesmen and the Situation Room and play resumed before all replays could be reviewed to confirm the off-side. The challenge by Columbus should have resulted in the Carolina goal being disallowed. Subsequently, Columbus was assessed a delay of game penalty. After confirmation in the intermission that the play was off-side, the remaining 0:45 of the delay of game penalty issued was rescinded to begin the third period.

Therefore, the Referees awarded Hurricanes forward Vincent Trocheck a goal according to Rule 63.6:"In the event that the goal post is displaced, either deliberately or accidentally, by a defending player, prior to the puck crossing the goal line between the normal position of the goalposts, the Referee may award a goal. In order to award a goal in this situation, the goal post must have been displaced by the actions of a defending player, the attacking player must have an imminent scoring opportunity prior to the goal post being displaced, and it must be determined that the puck would have entered the net between the normal position of the goal posts."

rulings.result_text: Call on the ice is overturned - No Goal Winnipeg
rulings.explanation: Video review determined Winnipeg's Kyle Connor used his arm to bat the puck, which caused the puck to illegally enter the Chicago net. According to Rule 78.5 (i), apparent goals shall be disallowed, "When the puck has been directed, batted or thrown into the net by an attacking player other than with a stick. When this occurs, if it is deemed to be done deliberately, then the decision shall be NO GOAL. A goal cannot be scored when the puck has been deliberately batted with any part of the attacking player's body into the net."

rulings.explanation: Following video review, the Referees determined Jacob Trouba pushed New Jersey's Blake Coleman into the New York net, which caused the net to become displaced from its moorings prior to the puck crossing the goal line. In order to award a goal in this situation, the goal post must have been displaced by the actions of a defending player, the attacking player must have an imminent scoring opportunity prior to the goal post being displaced, and it must be determined that the puck would have entered the net between the normal position of the goal posts."

rulings.result_text: Goal Vancouver

According to Rule 37.6, "Should the NHL Situation Room be able to determine that a goal has been scored through the use of video replay, and play on the ice has nonetheless continued, the NHL Situation Room shall instruct that the in-arena horn be sounded to stop play immediately, and the goal will be awarded. The game clock (and penalty clocks, if applicable) will then be re-set to the time of the goal."
Therefore, the clock is reset to show 16:11 (3:49 elapsed time) and good goal Vancouver.

The game clock (and penalty clocks, if applicable) will then be re-set to the time of the goal."
Therefore, the clock is reset to show 4:16 (15:44 elapsed time) and good goal Los Angeles.

At 4:16 of the third period in the Bruins/Hurricanes game, Boston requested a Coach's Challenge to review the "Interference on the Goalkeeper" decision that resulted in a "no goal" call.

After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Referees, the Situation Room confirmed that the actions of Bruins forward Jake DeBrusk impaired Hurricanes goaltender Curtis McElhinney's ability to play his position in the crease. According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a "GOAL" call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room (which shall include a former referee in the Officiating Department in the decision-making process), after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Referee who made the original call, determines that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4."Therefore, the original call stands - no goal Boston Bruins.Since the Coach's Challenge did not result in the original call being overturned, the Boston Bruins forfeit their time-out.

rulings.headline: Video Review: STL @ WPG - 13:52 of the Third Period
rulings.result_text: Good goal St. Louis
rulings.explanation: At 13:52 of the third period in the Blues/Jets game, the Referee initiated a video review to determine if the puck crossed the Winnipeg goal line between the normal positions of the goal posts. The original call on the ice was "no goal". The Situation Room informed the Referees that the puck entered the Winnipeg net between the normal position of the goal posts. The Referee then awarded the goal to St. Louis because of the actions of Dustin Byfuglien caused the Winnipeg net to become displaced as Brayden Schenn was in the act of shooting the puck into the Winnipeg net. The decision was made in relation to Rule 63.6 which states in part, "In order to award a goal in this situation, the goal post must have been displaced by the actions of a defending player, the puck must have been shot (or the player must be in the act of shooting) at the goal prior to the goal post being displaced, and it must be determined that the puck would have entered the net between the normal position of the goal posts." Good goal St. Louis.
rulings.description: Good goal St. Louis
rulings.basis: on-ice call no_goal (call_on_the_ice) vs final goal

rulings.headline: Coach's Challenge: TBL @ CBJ - 12:23 of the First Period
rulings.result_text: Call overturned, no goal Columbus
rulings.explanation:
At 12:23 of the first period in the Lightning/Blue Jackets game, Tampa Bay requested a Coach's Challenge to review whether the puck left the attacking zone prior to Cam Atkinson's goal.

After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Linesmen, the Situation Room determined that the puck left the attacking zone at 11:46 therefore the play was offside. According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a 'GOAL' call on the ice is that the Toronto Video Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an "Off-side" infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed."Therefore, the original call is overturned - no goal Columbus Blue Jackets.The clock is re-set to show 8:14 (11:46 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.
rulings.description: Call overturned, no goal Columbus
rulings.basis: result line: Call overturned, no goal Columbus

rulings.explanation:
At 7:30 of the third period in the Oilers/Avalanche game, Colorado requested a Coach's Challenge to review the "Interference on the Goalkeeper" decision that resulted in a "no goal" call.

After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Referees, the Situation Room determined that Colorado's Alexander Kerfoot was making a play on a loose puck and the puck entered the net in a legal fashion. The decision was made in accordance with Rule 69.7 which states, in part, that the goal on the ice should have been allowed because "in a rebound situation, or where a goalkeeper and attacking player(s) are simultaneously attempting to play a loose puck, whether inside or outside the crease, incidental contact will be permitted, and any goal that is scored as a result thereof will be allowed."Therefore the original call is overturned - good goal Colorado Avalanche.Since the Coach's Challenge did not result in the original call being overturned, the Colorado Avalanche retain their time-out.

At 9:43 of the third period in the Jets/Capitals game, Winnipeg requested a Coach's Challenge to review the "Interference on the Goalkeeper" decision that resulted in a "no goal" call.

At 17:31 of the third period in the Hurricanes/Predators game, Nashville requested a Coach's Challenge to review the "Interference on the Goalkeeper" decision that resulted in a "no goal" call.

After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Referee, the Situation Room determined that the actions of Carolina's Jordan Staal caused Nashville's Brian Boyle to contact Petr Mrazek before the puck crossed the goal line. rulings.result_text: Good Goal Ottawa Senators
rulings.explanation:
At 15:20 of the third period in the Senators/Islanders game, the immediate call by the Referee on the ice was good goal. The officials then huddled and determined that Ottawa's Brady Tkachuk interfered with New York's goaltender Robin Lehner prior to Jean-Gabriel Pageau's goal. Ottawa requested a Coach's Challenge to review the "Interference on the Goalkeeper" decision that resulted in a "no goal" call.

After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Referee, the Situation Room determined thatthe actions of New York's Brock Nelson caused Tkachuk to contact Lehner before the puck crossed the goal line. The decision was made in accordance with Note 2 of Rule 78.7 (ii) which states, in part, that the goal should be allowed because"the attacking Player was pushed, shoved or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper."Therefore, the original call is overturned - good goal Ottawa Senators.Since the Coach's Challenge resulted in the original call being overturned, the Ottawa Senators retain their time-out.

raw.headline: Coach's Challenge: PHI @ CBJ - 16:50 of the First Period
raw.body:
At 16:50 of the first period in the Flyers/Blue Jackets game, Columbus requested a Coach's Challenge to review whether Jakub Voracek was off-side prior to James van Riemsdyk's goal. After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, the Situation Room determined that **Voracek entered the attacking zone before the puck, without possession and control**.
Rule 83.1 states that, *"a player actually controlling the puck who shall cross the line ahead of the puck shall not be considered 'off-side,' provided he had possession and control of the puck prior to his skates crossing the blue line."* Voracek's entry did not meet this criteria.
**Therefore, the original call is overturned - no goal Philadelphia Flyers**.
The clock is re-set to show 3:26 (16:34 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.

After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Referee, the Situation Room confirmed that Wild forward [Joel Eriksson Ek](https://www.nhl.com/player/joel-eriksson-ek-8478493) was making a play on a loose puck, which entered the net in a legal fashion. Therefore, no goaltender interference infractions occurred. The decision was made in accordance with Rule 69.7 which states, in part, that the goal on the ice should have been allowed because "in a rebound situation, or where a goalkeeper and attacking player(s) are simultaneously attempting to play a loose puck, whether inside or outside the crease, incidental contact will be permitted, and any goal that is scored as a result thereof will be allowed."Therefore the original call stands - good goal Minnesota Wild.Since the Coach's Challenge did not result in the original call being overturned, the Winnipeg Jets forfeit their time-out.

rulings.result_text: No goal Anaheim
rulings.explanation:
At 19:15 of the third period in the Ducks/Oilers game, the Situation Room initiated a review under the terms of a Coach's Challenge to further examine a play at the Edmonton net.

After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Referee, the Situation Room supported the Referee's call on the ice that the actions of Adam Henrique impaired Mikko Koskinen's ability to defend his goal.According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a "GOAL" call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room (which shall include a former referee in the Officiating Department in the decision-making process), after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Referee who made the original call, determines that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4."Therefore the original call stands - no goal Anaheim Ducks.---  
NOTE: In the final minute of play in the third period and at any point in Overtime (Regular Season and Playoffs), Hockey Operations will initiate the review of any scenario that would otherwise be subject to a Coach's Challenge.
rulings.description: No goal Anaheim
rulings.basis: verdict sentence: call stands / confirmed

rulings.headline: Video Review: WPG @ COL - 1:57 of the Third Period
rulings.result_text: Good goal Winnipeg
rulings.explanation:
At 1:57 of the third period in the Jets/Avalanche game, the Situation Room initiated a video review to further examine a play at the Colorado net. Video review determined that Kyle Connor's original shot completely crossed the Colorado goal line as the culmination of a continuous play where the result was unaffected by the whistle.

The ruling was made in accordance with Rule 38.4 (ix), which reads in part, "The video review process shall be permitted to assist the Referees in determining the legitimacy of all potential goals… include situations whereby the Referee stops play or is in the process of stopping the play because he has lost sight of the puck and it is subsequently determined by video review that the puck crosses (or has crossed) the goal line and enters the net as the culmination of a continuous play where the result was unaffected by the whistle (i.e., the timing of the whistle was irrelevant to the puck entering the net at the end of a continuous play)."Good goal Winnipeg.
rulings.description: Good goal Winnipeg

At 14:19 of the second period in the Golden Knights/Lightning game, Tampa Bay requested a Coach's Challenge to review the "Interference on the Goalkeeper" decision that resulted in a "no goal" call. After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Referee, the Situation Room determined that**the actions of Vegas' Colin Miller caused Mathieu Joseph to contact Marc-Andre Fleury before the puck crossed the goal line.** The decision was made in accordance with Note 2 of Rule 78.7 (ii) which states, in part, that the goal should be allowed because "the attacking Player was pushed, shoved or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper."
**Therefore, the original call is overturned - good goal Tampa Bay Lightning.**
**Since the Coach's Challenge resulted in the original call being overturned, the Tampa Bay Lightning retain their time-out.**

At 6:57 of the second period in the Blackhawks/Rangers game, Chicago requested a Coach's Challenge to review whether New York was off-side prior to Mika Zibanejad's goal. After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, the Situation Room determined that **Zibanejad was off-side prior to his goal**. According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a 'GOAL' call on the ice is that the Toronto Video Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an "Off-side" infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed."
**Therefore, the original call is overturned - no goal New York Rangers.**
The clock is re-set to show 13:06 (6:54 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.

rulings.result_text: No goal Colorado
rulings.explanation:
At 10:04 of the third period in the Avalanche/Senators game, the Situation Room initiated a video review to determine if the puck entered the Ottawa net in a legal fashion.

The Situation Room determined that the goal frame was displaced because a goal peg was not in its respective hole in the ice. According to Rule 78.5 (x) which states: Apparent goals shall be disallowed "when the net becomes displaced accidentally.The goal frame is considered to be displaced if either or both pegs are no longer in their respective holes in the ice, or the net has completely come off one or both pegs, prior to or as the puck enters the goal." No goal Colorado.

rulings.explanation:
At 0:35 of the third period in the Canadiens/Avalanche game, Montreal requested a Coach's Challenge to review whether Gabriel Landeskog interfered with goaltender Carey Price prior to his goal.

After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Referee, the Situation Room confirmed that the contact between Colorado's Landeskog and Price did not impair the goaltender's ability to defend his goal and had no discernible impact on the play. The decision was made in accordance with Rule 78.7 (ii, b) that states in part, that the goal on the ice should have been allowed because "the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal, and in fact, had no discernible impact on the play". After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, the Situation Room determined that Luff was off-side prior to the goal. rulings.headline: Coach's Challenge: VGK @ OTT - 12:00 of the Third Period
rulings.result_text: Original call stands - good goal Vegas Golden Knights
rulings.explanation:
At 12:00 of the third period in the Golden Knights/Senators game, Ottawa requested a Coach's Challenge to review whether Vegas' William Carrier interfered with goaltender Craig Anderson prior to Pierre-Edouard Bellemare's goal.

After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Referee, the Situation Room determined that Anderson initiated contact with Carrier, who was outside the crease prior to the goal. Therefore no goaltender interference infractions occurred. The decision was made in accordance with Rule 69.7 which states, in part, that the goal on the ice should have been allowed because "in a rebound situation, or where a goalkeeper and attacking player(s) are simultaneously attempting to play a loose puck, whether inside or outside the crease, incidental contact will be permitted, and any goal that is scored as a result thereof will be allowed."Therefore the original call stands - good goal Vegas Golden Knights.Since the Coach's Challenge did not result in the original call being overturned, the Ottawa Senators forfeit their time-out.

rulings.result_text: Call overturned, no goal Colorado
rulings.explanation:
At 7:39 of the third period in the Predators/Avalanche game, Nashville requested a Coach's Challenge to review whether Colorado was off-side prior to Colin Wilson's goal.

After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, the Situation Room determined that Alexander Kerfoot was off-side prior to the goal. According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a 'GOAL' call on the ice is that the Toronto Video Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an "Off-side" infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed."Therefore, the original call is overturned - no goal Colorado Avalanche.The clock is re-set to show 12:33 (7:27 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.

Good goal Colorado.

rulings.headline: Video Review: PIT @ TOR - 18:25 of the Third Period
rulings.result_text: No goal Toronto
rulings.explanation:
At 18:25 of the third period in the Penguins/Maple Leafs game, the Situation Room initiated a video review because the puck entered the Pittsburgh net. The Referee informed the Situation Room that he was in the process of blowing his whistle to stop play before the puck crossed the goal line. The decision was made in accordance of Rule 31.2 which states, in part, that "the Referee may deem the play to be stopped slightly prior to the whistle actually being blown. The fact that the puck may come loose or cross the goal line prior to the sound of the whistle has no bearing if the Referee has ruled that the play had been stopped prior to this happening."

Additionally, Rule 78.5 states that apparent goals shall be disallowed "when the Referee deems the play has been stopped, even if he had not physically had the opportunity to stop play by blowing his whistle." This is not a reviewable play therefore the Referee's call on the ice stands - no goal Toronto.

Good goal Washington.

rulings.headline: Coach's Challenge: VGK @ WPG - 7:35 of the First Period
rulings.result_text: Call overturned, good goal Winnipeg
rulings.explanation:
At 7:35 of the first period in the Golden Knights/Jets game, Winnipeg requested a Coach's Challenge to review the "Interference on the Goalkeeper" decision that resulted in a "no goal" call.

After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Referee, the Situation Room determined that the contact between Winnipeg's Joel Armia and Vegas goaltender Marc-Andre Fleury occurred after the puck was deflected into the net and, therefore, no goaltender interference infractions occurred. According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a "NO GOAL" call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room (which shall include a former referee in the Officiating Department in the decision-making process), after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Referee who made the original call, determines that the goal on the ice should have been allowed because either: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by the attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play."Therefore, the original call is overturned - good goal Winnipeg Jets.Since the Coach's Challenge resulted in the original call being overturned, the Jets retain their time-out.
rulings.description: Call overturned, good goal Winnipeg
rulings.basis: result line: Call overturned, good goal Winnipeg

After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Referee, the Situation Room determined that **contact between Vegas' Jonathan Marchessault and Jones prevented him from his job**, in accordance with Rule 78.7 which states in part: "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a "GOAL" call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room (which shall include a former referee in the Officiating Department in the decision-making process), after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Referee who made the original call, determines that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4."
Rule 69.1 states that goals should be disallowed if "an attacking player, either by his positioning or by contact, impairs the goalkeeper's ability to move freely within his crease or defend his goal."
**Therefore the original call is overturned - no goal Vegas Golden Knights.** **Rule 78.7: Coach's Challenge**
A team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios:
**1. "Off-Side" Play Leading to a Goal**
A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-side" infraction by the attacking team.
**New for 2017-18**: If the result of the challenge is that the play was "On-side", the goal shall count and the team that issued the challenge shall be assessed a minor penalty for delaying the game.
**2. Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"**
A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; or
A play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.
**Updated for 2017-18:** A team may only request a Coach's Challenge for Interference on the Goalkeeper if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.

raw.headline: Coach's Challenge: NSH @ COL - 17:37 of the Second Period
raw.body:
At 17:37 of the second period in the Predators/Avalanche game, Colorado requested a Coach's Challenge to review the "Interference on the Goalkeeper" decision that resulted in a "no goal" call.
After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Referee, the Situation Room **confirmed the "no goal" call because the presence and subsequent contact in the crease between Colorado's Carl Soderberg and Nashville's Pekka Rinne prevented the goaltender from doing his job.**
Therefore the original call stands - **no goal Colorado Avalanche.**
Since the Coach's Challenge did not result in the original call being overturned, **the Avalanche forfeit their time-out.** **Rule 78.7: Coach's Challenge**
A team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios:
**1. "Off-Side" Play Leading to a Goal**
A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-side" infraction by the attacking team.
**New for 2017-18**: If the result of the challenge is that the play was "On-side", the goal shall count and the team that issued the challenge shall be assessed a minor penalty for delaying the game.
**2. Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"**
A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; or
A play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.
**Updated for 2017-18**: A team may only request a Coach's Challenge for Interference on the Goalkeeper if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.

raw.headline: Coach's Challenge: CAR @ OTT - 17:19 of the Second Period
raw.body:
At 17:19 of the second period in the Hurricanes/Senators game, Ottawa requested a Coach's Challenge to review whether Carolina was off-side prior to their goal. After reviewing all available replays and consulting with NHL Hockey Operations staff, the Linesman determined that **the Hurricanes tagged up and entered the attacking zone legally prior to the goal.**
Since the Coach's Challenge did not result in the original call being overturned, **the Ottawa Senators are assessed a minor penalty for delaying the game.**
---
**Rule 78.7: Coach's Challenge** A team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios:
**1. "Off-Side" Play Leading to a Goal** A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-side" infraction by the attacking team.
**New for 2017-18:** If the result of the challenge is that the play was "On-side", the goal shall count and the team that issued the challenge shall be assessed a minor penalty for delaying the game.
**2. Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"** A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; or
A play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.
**Updated for 2017-18:** A team may only request a Coach's Challenge for Interference on the Goalkeeper if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.

raw.headline: Coach's Challenge: MTL @ FLA - 3:30 of the Third Period
raw.body:
At 3:30 of the third period in the Canadiens/Panthers game, Florida requested a Coach's Challenge to review whether Montreal's Jacob de la Rose interfered with goaltender Roberto Luongo prior to Paul Byron's goal.
After reviewing all available replays and consulting with NHL Hockey Operations staff, the Referee determined that **de la Rose interfered with Luongo before the puck crossed the goal line.** According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a 'GOAL' call on the ice is that the Referee, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Toronto Video Room, determines that the goal should have been disallowed due to 'Interference on the Goalkeeper,' as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4."
**Therefore the original call is overturned - no goal Montreal Canadiens.**
Since the Coach's Challenge resulted in the original call being overturned, **the Florida Panthers retain their time-out.** **Rule 78.7: Coach's Challenge**
A team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios:
**1. "Off-Side" Play Leading to a Goal**
A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-side" infraction by the attacking team.
**New for 2017-18**: If the result of the challenge is that the play was "On-side", the goal shall count and the team that issued the challenge shall be assessed a minor penalty for delaying the game.
**2. Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"**
A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; or
A play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.
**Updated for 2017-18**: A team may only request a Coach's Challenge for Interference on the Goalkeeper if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.
